<reason>Both sides executed at a high level in a genuinely philosophical clash. B's strongest work was the burden framework and the demolition of A's gambler case (the risk was disclosed on every page; "fraud without words" is not fraud), plus the crispest closing of the debate ("they are not standards consent must meet from outside; they are what consent is"). But B's route required narrowing the motion to "consent between the transacting parties," an evasive reframing of the proposition as written. A's structural-dependence externality argument (a deal that only exists because waste is dumped has the harm baked into its terms) was never fully dissolved by B's "separate wrong" carve-up, and A cleanly won the paternalism clash by separating ethical verdicts from policy remedies, with the lying-to-a-friend analogy effectively answering B's "name the wronged party" demand. A also answered both pressure questions directly with real distinctions (delivering wanted value vs. extracting value via engineered error). Costs on both sides: A's closing slightly misdescribed B's definition (adding "decent alternatives" B had explicitly rejected), and B was clipped in three turns. On the motion as written, A retains a live route B only answered by swapping in a narrower question, giving A a clear but competitive edge.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The exchange over the gambler case: A's Q1 dilemma about whether "competence" secretly requires bias-immunity forced B to choose, and B's Rebuttal 2 answer — that the gambler read every page, wanted the derivative, and that fraud requires false representation — was the sharpest single counter of the debate. A's rejoinder that B's framework "waves through deliberate exploitation of known cognitive weaknesses" kept the point alive, but B's reply landed more cleanly.</best_rebuttal>
